summary: Shows the security problems that come from allowing overlapping fragments in IPv6, and updates the base IPv6 specification to explicitly forbid them. Receivers must handle such packets as the document describes. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If puzzle pieces overlap in strange ways, an attacker can trick you about the picture. This document says that IPv6 pieces must not overlap, closing a loophole for sneaky traffic.

questions: why are overlapping fragments a security risk
what happens to overlapping ipv6 fragments
how do overlapping fragments bypass a firewall
subtitle: IPv6 fragments must not overlap, because overlap lets an attacker slip past firewalls.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 fragmentation algorithm did not prevent fragments from overlapping, which lets an attacker rewrite parts of a packet after a firewall has inspected it.
tldr.mechanism: Senders MUST NOT create overlapping fragments, and a receiver that finds an overlap MUST silently discard the whole datagram, including fragments not yet received.
tldr.outcome: The rule closes a firewall bypass. RFC 6946 later updated this document.

today: RFC 5722 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2460 and has itself been updated by RFC 6946. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Overlapping Fragments
sections.content:
IPv6 uses fragmentation when a packet will not fit inside the path MTU. The sender uses a fragment header, defined in Section 4.5 of RFC 2460, to split the datagram into smaller fragments, and the destination reassembles them.

The algorithm in RFC 2460 does not prevent fragments from overlapping. That can cause security problems with firewalls. RFC 5722 explores the issue and updates the IPv6 specification to forbid overlapping fragments explicitly.
sections.eli5: A big parcel is split into smaller boxes and put back together at the end. Nothing said the boxes could not overlap.

sections.title: Why the IPv4 Defence Falls Short
sections.content:
Common firewalls use the algorithm in RFC 1858 to catch malicious packets that overwrite parts of the transport-layer header to dodge inbound connection checks. For TCP, RFC 1858 recommends dropping packets with a fragment offset of 1.

That works for IPv4 but not for IPv6. The fragmentable part of an IPv6 packet can have extension headers in front of the TCP header, so the offset check is less effective.
sections.eli5: The old guard watched one particular door. In IPv6 there are more doors, so watching just that one is not enough.

sections.title: The Attack
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a packet split in two. The first fragment holds an 80-octet destination options header followed by a TCP header with the SYN and ACK flags set. A stateful firewall may take this for a reply to a connection started on the trusted side and let it through, along with later fragments that share the same Fragment Identification value.

The attacker then sends a second fragment that overlaps the TCP header and sets SYN=1 and ACK=0. After reassembly the receiver sees a new connection request instead of a reply, so the firewall's access control has been bypassed.

The RFC says this is more serious in IPv6 than in IPv4. In IPv4 the overlapping part of the TCP header does not include the source and destination ports, but in IPv6 an overlapping fragment can easily replace either port.
sections.eli5: The attacker shows the guard a harmless-looking first piece, then slips in a second piece that covers part of it and changes what it says.

sections.title: Required Node Behavior
sections.content:
Nodes sending datagrams that need fragmenting MUST NOT create overlapping fragments.

When reassembling, if one or more fragments is found to overlap, the entire datagram MUST be silently discarded. That includes any fragments already received and any that have not yet arrived. Nodes MAY also track these events, for instance with counters or alarms.
sections.eli5: If any two pieces overlap, throw the whole puzzle away without saying anything, and keep count if you like.

sections.title: The Example Fragments in Detail
sections.content:
The RFC draws both fragments of its example. Each carries a fragment header whose Next Header value is DOH(60) and whose Identification is aaaabbbb. The first has Fragment Offset 0 and the more-fragments bit set to 1; the second has Fragment Offset 10 and that bit set to 0.

The first fragment holds the destination options header with Next Header TCP(6) and HdrExtLen 9, then the TCP header. The second fragment begins with its own TCP header at its offset, which is why the two overlap and the later bytes can replace the flags the firewall saw.
sections.eli5: Both pieces carry the same label, so they get glued together, but the second piece sits on top of part of the first and changes it.
